headlines.title: Brent Oil Tops $100 as US-Iran War Shows Little Sign of Abating
headlines.summary: So, one: Brent crude has crossed $100 for the first time since July, which is the kind of round number that functions less as an economic data point and more as a psychological alarm clock for every asset class simultaneously (bonds, equities, currencies — all of them now awake and unhappy). Two: the proximate cause is the US military destroying five Iranian tankers, which Iran has responded to by attacking merchant vessels near the Strait of Hormuz, which carries roughly 20% of global oil supply through a body of water that is, and this is the funny part if you squint, apparently still open for business but only barely. Energy stocks catch a bid, airlines and industrials get repriced, and the Fed — which was maybe going to pause — now has to have a very awkward conversation about whether $100 oil is 'transitory' (a word they have sworn never to use again, and yet).

headlines.title: Treasuries Weaken as Rising Oil Prices Boost Rate-Hike Bets
headlines.summary: The bond market, which had been doing its best impression of a calm person in a waiting room, is now actively selling off as traders reprice the probability of a Fed rate hike as soon as next week — which is, structurally, the kind of thing that makes every duration-sensitive asset on the planet reconsider its life choices at once. The five-spots-to-watch piece from earlier in the feed was already flagging the creep toward 5% on the 10-year; now with oil at $100 feeding directly into inflation expectations, that creep has become something closer to a jog (and mortgage rates, per the Bloomberg piece, are already at a one-year-plus high of 6.85%, which is its own separate disaster for housing). Equities broadly, and rate-sensitive sectors like utilities, REITs, and long-duration tech specifically, are the transmission mechanism here.

headlines.title: U.S. reveals import ban on slew of Canadian goods as trade war escalates
headlines.summary: Canada's CA$27.6 billion in retaliatory tariffs (doubling steel and aluminum duties to 50%) are now live, and the US has responded with import bans on motorcycles, alcohol, and dairy products effective September 29th — which is the kind of escalation ladder that, if you described it to someone in 2019, they would assume you were summarizing a satirical novel. The affected sectors are genuinely broad: steel and aluminum producers get a complicated mixed signal (protected domestically, but supply-chain costs rise), consumer staples with Canadian exposure get hit, and the auto sector (already navigating the Bombardier drama) faces renewed input cost anxiety. The September 29 effective date gives markets exactly three weeks to decide whether to price this in gradually or all at once, and historically they tend to choose 'all at once, at the worst possible moment.'
